text: Cassini wasn't sterile, and that's the reason the final plunge into Saturn matters. I guess if it drifted and struck a moon, especially Enceladus, which people think might have a habitable ocean, Earth microbes could hitch a ride, and that would mess with future biological surveys. I'd say plunging into Saturn's upper atmosphere is the safest way to make sure it can't hit anything. That final dive was designed to break the spacecraft apart, so it's gone and can't contaminate the moons. I suppose a controlled crash into the planet is just the cleanest place to put a dirty spacecraft.

I think most people are focusing on the wrong leg. When you push, the leg that stays on the board is doing a lot more than looking stationary. It has to carry your balance, absorb the impact of every push, and keep you from tipping, and I have noticed my own non-pushing leg aches after a while for that reason. I am not saying the board is broken, but I would check your stance first. If you are leaning too far to one side or pushing with a very uneven rhythm, one leg is going to take a bigger share of the load. That surprised me the first time I realized it, because it feels like the pushing leg should be doing all the work.

As far as I know, the pain can show up in the hip, knee, or ankle, and I would say the ankle is common because the stationary leg is often braced. I ask myself whether I am locking that joint, and often the answer is yes. I have found that loosening up, shortening the push, and keeping the board moving in a steadier cadence helps. If the pain persists, I would get it looked at, because a small strain can make the stationary leg ache every time you ride.

I’d say the premise is a little off: most Black people in the US aren’t called Afro-American, they’re usually Black American or African American. I think “Afro-American” is a narrower label, used to point to African ancestry or the African diaspora, not to say everyone is literally from Africa. As far as I know, the word is often a cultural or political term: it’s about where your people came from, not where you were born. That’s why someone can be Black American and still be described as Afro-American if their lineage connects to Africa, even if they’ve never lived there. I guess the confusion comes from treating “Afro-American” as the only correct name for all Black people. It isn’t. In everyday usage, “African American” is more common, and it works as a broad category. “Afro-American” is the one that carries that extra emphasis on African roots, and I’d say it’s closer to an identity label than a census category. So the short answer is: they’re not “from Africa” in the sense of being born or living there, but the term is about descent, and most Black Americans have some African ancestry. That’s my take; I’d hedge that labels are personal.

I think the short answer is that Syrians get weapons from several nearby places at once. I'd say the biggest flows come from Iraq, Turkey, Iran, and Lebanon, along with global black-market channels; some are also produced or assembled locally. I'm not sure how much is home-made, but smuggling routes matter. As for why they still get them, I guess it's because the conflict keeps opening new fronts, so factions need fresh guns and ammunition. Neighbors and external backers also push their own sides. Even in places with ceasefires, the supply continues because nobody has agreed who controls the weapons.

I think the short answer is that intense pleasure and no adverse effects are a tough trade. Can a drug give euphoria with zero adverse effects? I doubt it. Drugs like heroin or coke don't just add a separate "happy" switch. They hit the same brain reward and stress systems the body already uses for food, sex, safety, and recovery. Push that system hard and the body compensates. That compensation is where the downsides come from. I guess the body doesn't see a drug as a gift; it sees a disturbance. If a substance floods your reward circuitry, your own natural chemistry steps down. That's a feedback loop, not a moral failing. You stop enjoying ordinary things as much, and the drug becomes necessary just to feel normal. The good effects aren't isolated. Strong stimulation or depression changes heart rate, breathing, sleep, appetite, and alertness. With heroin, the part that feels good is also the part that can slow breathing. With coke, the excitement raises heart and blood pressure. A drug with zero adverse effects would have to touch almost nothing outside the pleasure system, and I'm not sure the brain is built that way. Pleasure systems are woven into eating, sleep, fear, and recovery. I'd also push back on "all drugs are bad". Some drugs are used medically because they help with pain, mood, breathing, or sleep. The problem is usually the dose and how often you take it. A drug that feels great at a low dose and harms you at a high dose isn't automatically bad. The issue is that the very feeling you're after is the mechanism that later drives tolerance and dependence. I don't think a perfect pleasure drug is impossible in principle, but I think it is very unlikely. The brain has to balance reward with survival. If a substance gives a huge spike, the system rebalances. That's why pleasure drugs come with costs: the costs are the same circuitry doing its job. I've also noticed that "bad" often means the dose or the timing is off, and that matters more than the drug itself. As far as I know, the body keeps correcting for the spike, and that correction is where the unpleasant side effects live. People vary too. I've noticed the same drug can be manageable for one person and dangerous for another, and that's why the "all drugs are bad" line is too coarse.

Hi [Name],

I think it could be a mix of tension, poor posture, dehydration, and fatigue, but since you say it is different from your normal headaches, I wouldn't just write it off. I'd get it checked by a doctor so they can rule out anything more serious. Does it happen mostly in your head, or is it all over? Have you noticed if it gets worse after walking for a while? Try drinking water and taking breaks. Your pain is real, and your body may be reacting to the physical strain of a long day out.

Talk soon,
[Your name]

Hi,
Thanks for sending this. I think what happened is a mental slip caused by your brother's little trick. As far as I know, saying “silk” five times and spelling it can leave your brain stuck on that word. Then when he asks what cows drink, your memory automatically supplies the word most strongly tied to cows: milk. Cows do drink water, but milk is the first thing most people connect with them, so it comes out without much checking. I'd say it's more a test of automatic associations than a memory test. It is not a sign you are confused or weak. It is just an associative slip, the same kind of mistake people make when they say “blue” when they mean “red” because the words feel connected. Let me know if you want, I can send a short explanation of semantic priming and how these quick tests work.
Best,
Sam

Hi Sam,

I am glad you asked. House buying is not a standard purchase. I think the part people get wrong is treating it like buying a car. I would tell you to start with your actual monthly budget, not the house price. My guess is you should leave room for property tax, insurance, maintenance, and the unexpected stuff. As far as I know, get a pre-approval for a mortgage before looking, because it tells you what you can really afford. I have seen people fall in love with a house and then be surprised by the total cost of owning it.

I would also say look carefully at the street, the neighbours, and how the house behaves in bad weather. I think that is where the real problems show up. Do not skip the survey. If you are in a rush, make it a full structural survey, not just a basic one. I have a feeling that the legal side is boring but important. Ask your lawyer to explain the title, covenants, and any leases. If a friend is helping you, I would not let them make the financial call for you. Call me if you want help.

Best,
Alex

Hi,

I think the short answer is that a 3-in-1 isn't three separate products in one bottle, but a single blended formulation designed to clean skin and hair at the same time. I'd say the difference is mostly about surfactants and conditioning agents. Bodywashes use mild surfactants suited to skin, shampoos use ones that lather and remove scalp oils, and conditioners add fats or silicones to smooth hair. A 3-in-1 has to compromise: it can't be as strong as a dedicated shampoo or as rich as a dedicated conditioner. A 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner already blends cleaning and smoothing for hair. Adding bodywash into that mix means the formula is tuned more toward the whole body, with fragrance and skin-friendly cleansers. I asked myself whether this is just marketing, and I think part of it is. The 3-in-1 is a convenience product, not a replacement for specialized care. As far as I know, it's usually not as effective as separate products, but it's convenient. I guess if you have normal hair and skin, it's fine for a quick wash. If your hair is very dry or your scalp needs real treatment, I'd still use separate products.

Cheers,
Me

Hi,

Good question, and honestly one of those things that is more complicated than it looks. I'm not a geologist, but I've read enough to understand the basic idea.

The short answer is GPS. People set up receivers on the ground, and the satellites let them pin down position to within a few centimetres. Then you just take the difference between where a point was a year ago and where it is now. Divide by the time and you have a speed, usually quoted in millimetres per year. I think that is the core of it.

I guess what surprises people is that continents move slowly, so you need to wait. A single month is not enough to see much. You need repeated measurements over a long time, and then the motion becomes clear.

I have read that they also use other tricks, like looking at coastlines and tide gauges, but GPS is really the workhorse here. It is also the reason why a point on the North American plate can be said to be drifting at a few millimetres a year without anyone having to wait a decade to see it happen.

Does that clear it up for you?

Cheers,

Quick note. I think the key point is that inbreeding doesn't add a new inherited low IQ gene. It mainly increases the chance that two parents carry the same harmful recessive mutations. If both pass one, the offspring can end up with two copies and show problems. For intelligence, the effect is cumulative, and many small-effect variants plus rare recessive alleles can each nudge cognitive ability down. Close relatives are more likely to share those variants. I'd say that explains the average drop, not a single cause. As far as I know, the risk is not only about IQ; it also raises the chance of congenital disorders and developmental problems. So I guess the science is less about inbreeding lowering IQ directly and more about making hidden genetic risks visible. That is why offspring of closely related parents can have lower average scores, but individual results vary a lot.

What surprises me is that the arm isn't a shield; it mostly has a lot of soft tissue and is farther from the chest. I think most of the pain difference comes from padding and distance from vital areas. A hit or cut in the upper arm or forearm often lands on muscle and fat, and the body reads that as less urgent than a blow to the torso or head. I guess that explains why people downplay an arm injury when something happens near the torso.

I'd say pain isn't just tissue damage. It is also how the nervous system flags the location. The arm has fewer survival warnings, so the brain tends to make the hurt feel smaller. As far as I know, this does not mean an arm injury is safe. If the wound is deep, or you can't move the arm well, I think it still needs checking.

The part that always catches me is that carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless, so you can breathe it in without noticing. I think the real problem is how it interacts with hemoglobin in red blood cells. CO binds to hemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen, which means the blood's ability to carry oxygen drops. Tissues then don't get enough oxygen, and that's where the danger starts.

I'd say that this is different from carbon dioxide in a way that is easy to miss. CO2 is normal to breathe in small amounts, and the body is set up to move it out through the lungs. It is the waste gas we exhale, and I guess most people don't think about it because it's part of ordinary breathing. It can become harmful if concentrations get high, but for normal exposure it doesn't block oxygen the way CO does.

As far as I know, that distinction matters most for a new colleague. CO does not simply make you sleepy the way high CO2 can. I think the reason it feels more poisonous is that it directly interferes with oxygen delivery, while CO2 mainly sits in the blood and is cleared normally. I also think it's worth noting that carbon monoxide can build up in poorly ventilated spaces, which is why alarms matter. I guess the practical point for the team is that CO is the one you have to actively watch for, because it doesn't give you the obvious warning signs that high CO2 sometimes does.

I would add that this is also why CO can be dangerous in enclosed spaces where exhaust fumes don't get diluted quickly. I'm not saying CO2 is harmless, only that the everyday breathing contrast is why CO gets the stronger warning label.

I'd say the most misunderstood thing about the brace position is that it does not keep you safe from the impact. I think its value is much smaller: it changes how your body meets the stop. In a hard landing or crash, your body wants to keep moving while the aircraft stops. The brace turns that uncontrolled forward motion into a controlled, bent-knee stop. I guess that is why passengers are told to bend their knees and keep their feet flat on the floor. If you can grip the seat or controls, you have a handle on how your upper body reacts. Holding your feet and bending your knees lets the shock travel through legs rather than through your spine, and keeping the head back or arms crossed helps protect the face, neck, and airway. I know some people think the position is only for a crash landing, but I think it matters for any sudden stop, such as an emergency landing where the aircraft halts quickly. I'm not saying it makes a crash harmless. I'd say it mostly reduces the chance of broken bones, head injury, or organs jolting around. In other words, the position does not avoid the emergency; it helps the body absorb the stop in a way that is less likely to hurt you badly.

I think the question hides a trap. We treat "well known" as today's global recognition, and a pre-industrial firm's local fame doesn't count the same way. As far as I know, most pre-industrial businesses were workshops, trading houses, or guild firms, and their reach was local or regional. That surprised me because we imagine ancient firms as timeless brands, but most didn't survive or leave enough records for us to name them. Industrialization changed things with mass production and mass media, so later famous firms could become visible. I'd say the real issue is what counts as "well known" now, rather than whether old businesses existed.

I still think the bank is usually the cheaper route, and the reason is less about the interest rate itself and more about what the dealership quietly piles into the loan. A dealer can advertise a lower APR, but that lower rate often comes bundled with dealer add-ons: a doc fee, a dealer prep fee, an extended warranty, a maintenance package, or a gap or service contract. If those items are financed, you are paying interest on money the dealership gets to keep, not on the car. I’ve seen the pattern often enough to suspect the rate is a hook. The bank may quote a higher rate, but the loan is usually just the car. No surprise fees, no forced service plan, no 'must-buy' insurance, and you can see exactly what you are paying for. That transparency is worth more than a point or two of interest.

There is also a behavioral piece here. Dealerships control the paperwork room, and the total cost is easier to hide when many line items are stacked together. A bank forces the borrower to compare a single loan amount, a single rate, and a single payoff. The lower dealer rate can be real, but it is not the whole story. If the dealership includes a two-year maintenance contract or a $750 doc fee in the financed amount, the borrower ends up paying interest on all of it. The bank route keeps the principal close to the actual vehicle price.

I would not automatically choose the dealer just because their rate looks better. I’d pull both quotes and compare total payments, not just the APR. That means looking at the principal, the fees, and any add-ons, then doing the math over the loan term. In my experience, the bank can win on total cost even with a higher nominal rate. The dealership’s lower rate is often offset, or more than offset, by the costs they add. If the bank’s extra interest is small compared with the dealer’s hidden fees, the bank is the smarter choice. I’m not saying dealers are always bad, but I’m saying the advertised rate is not the full price. I’d rather finance through the bank, because it is easier to verify and harder to pad. I also like that I can pay the bank early without fighting a dealer who wants me to keep the add-ons, and then stop.

I keep coming back to how uneven the map is, and honestly I don’t mind the patchwork as much as I used to. I think letting states experiment is one of the better things about how this has played out. California and Colorado both ended up legalizing, but they got there through different routes and ended up with different rules, and that variation is useful to watch. As far as I know, federal law still treats marijuana as illegal in most cases, which creates this weird gap where your state says yes and the feds say no. I’d say that gap is the part that surprises me most, and I guess it’s why people keep asking about it. I’m not sure I have the whole picture, but from where I’m standing, I’d rather have states figure this out piece by piece than have one federal rule for everyone.

I think our body's "electricity" comes from ions moving across cell membranes. Nerves and muscles use sodium and potassium to keep the inside of cells at a negative voltage. When a neuron fires, ion channels open, sodium rushes in, and that tiny shift travels along the axon. In muscle, the same signal starts contraction. I'd say it's a chemical-physical process. I guess people imagine a battery inside us. The real story is ions, proteins, and membrane potentials. As far as I know, the heart uses similar ion-channel logic to keep beating. I find that genuinely cool, and honestly, it works.

I think people often treat sampling like a mystery, but to me it is mostly digging, cutting, and listening. The question asks how musicians sample older songs, and my take is that the process is less about magic and more about patience and a few technical moves. I have spent way too many hours in record stores and online archives, and I would say the first step is always finding the source. That can mean hunting for a 1970s soul record, a jazz pressing, or a forgotten TV theme. You are looking for a moment in the song, usually a drum break, a bass line, or a vocal phrase, that still has energy when played alone.

Once you have the record or file, you pull out the part you want. In my own work I usually import the audio into a DAW and then slice the section into small pieces. I do not try to copy the whole song. I take a short phrase and make it fit my tempo, either by time stretching or by cutting and rearranging. This is where the old song starts to become part of a new one. If the sample is too slow, I speed it up; if it is too fast, I slow it down. The trick is to keep it from sounding stretched or broken.

I would also say that people underestimate the legal side. If you are releasing commercially, there are two layers: rights in the composition and rights in the master recording. A mechanical license may cover the composition, but the master use license is for the actual recording. I have seen projects stall over this, so I think it is worth handling early, not after the song is finished. In my experience, many smaller labels will work with you, but you need to ask before you think the track is done.

What I find most interesting is that sampling is a conversation across decades. You are not just stealing a sound; you are giving an old song a second life in a new context. A drum break from an older record can suddenly become the heartbeat of a new track. I am not saying that makes every sample legitimate, but I do think the best examples feel like dialogue rather than theft. The musician has to make the borrowed piece work with their own rhythm and mood, not just paste it in as decoration. That is the part I care about. A sample can be lazy if it simply sits there, but when it is cut, shifted, and rebuilt, it becomes a living element. I would not say every older song is waiting to be sampled, and I would not say every sample is automatically good. But for me, the most exciting moment is when an old fragment suddenly clicks with a new idea, and the past stops feeling distant.

My head hurts because the stuff around the brain is being irritated, not the brain itself. I think this is what people get wrong: the brain doesn't feel pain, so when I get a headache the pain is coming from blood vessels, the brain's coverings, or the nerves and muscles in the head. A tension headache starts as a tight band around my temples and the back of my neck. I'd say stress and bad posture keep those muscles tight until they start aching. Migraines are different. I've had them, and they feel like a throb that follows a blood-vessel rhythm. It is not that my brain is hurt; it is the trigeminal nerve and tissue reacting to changes in blood flow and inflammation. That is exactly why I stop working, lie down, and take paracetamol. The pain is very real, but it always comes from outside the brain's tissue.

I can't even say the food was good because we never got to eat. We got there at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, picked this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and thought it'd be easy. We put our names in their completely useless digital waitlist and were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15 p.m. It was just a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait stretches that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn't totally wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if that were an option at all.

I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so when this buffet had them, that caught my attention. I went there on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and there was no line at all, which surprised me. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. I had figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse, but afterward I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

Honestly, I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but I feel like those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

I'd say four stars, and I'm keeping it. The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then; example becomes eexample and I backspace. It happens to me maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while waiting. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I've been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well, the under-21 version of it, so I've seen a lot of shows before I could gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed, maybe slightly worse than mixed. The good part: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You're looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view, rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too, the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil, not exactly a rip-off, just that if you've seen Cirque, you've seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity. Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don't know. There's a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it's trying to say. Also, there's way too much happening at once: too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle, more must be better, so they crammed everything in. Ticket note: if you're staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125, and that helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn't pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn't blown away, and I don't think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you've never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don't expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago I ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear, and we ordered them by phone. The shirts never got here, and I guess I did not learn about it until several weeks later. The sales rep wrote the address wrong, reading her own “7” as a “1,” so instead of 5407 the package went to 5401. The people at 5401 took it to the local UPS store to return it. Then it disappeared and nobody heard anything more. During the dispute we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the first two. The owner took over then. He admitted the wrong address but said no refund until the shirts came back. He also blamed us partly for not being friendly enough to the people at 5401, four doors away. I still think it odd that they held out. We disputed the original charge with our card company, and eventually got a credit.
